t: The Signature Strap Roll: Pre-Marked Cut Lines
title: The Signature Strap Roll: Pre-Marked Cut Lines
description: The Signature strap roll prints cut marks every 2 inches along the roll edge, with the common PC sizes highlighted — 4-inch fan straps, 6-inch trunk straps, 9-inch PSU straps. You cut on the marks instead of measuring, so every strap comes out the right size and the roll yields a predictable strap count. It is a small printing choice that removes measuring from the most common cuts.

t: Signature Strap Width System: Three Rolls, No Guessing
title: Signature Strap Width System: Three Rolls, No Guessing
description: The Signature system standardizes three rolls — 1/2-inch blue for thin wire bundles, 3/4-inch black for general trunks, 1-inch red for PSU mains — and the width IS the label. Grab blue for fans, black for everything standard, red for power. The color-width pairing means you never measure a bundle to choose a strap; the job tells you the roll.

demo.program:
rolls = [("1/2 in BLUE", "thin wires: fans, front-panel"),
         ("3/4 in BLACK", "general trunks (the default)"),
         ("1 in RED", "PSU mains")]
for r, use in rolls:
    print(f"  {r:<14} -> {use}")
print("Width IS the label: the job picks the roll, no measuring.")

t: Signature Trunk Cards: The Routing Map
title: Signature Trunk Cards: The Routing Map
description: Every Signature build gets a trunk card — a small diagram showing each cable trunk, its color code, strap positions, and service loop locations. The card tapes inside the side panel, so the next person to open the case sees the intended routing instead of guessing. Cable management becomes documented infrastructure, not one builder's memory.

print("  - service loop locations noted")

title: Signature Service-Loop Standard
description: The Signature standard puts a service loop on every trunk: 4 inches at the source end, folded flat, strapped with a contrasting-color strap so loops are findable. The trunk card records each loop's location. Upgrades draw from loops first; only when loops are exhausted does anyone re-route. It is the difference between a case that welcomes upgrades and one that fights them.

demo.program:
print("Standard: 4-in loop, folded flat, contrasting strap, on the trunk card.")
print("Upgrade rule: draw from loops FIRST; re-route only when loops exhausted.")
print("A case that welcomes upgrades vs one that fights them.")

title: Signature vs Generic Rolls
description: A generic roll is unmarked strap you measure and cut by eye. The Signature roll is pre-marked, width-color-coded, and comes with anchors and trunk cards — the measuring, labeling, and documenting are built into the product. Both hold cables; only one carries the system. For a shop, the time saved on measuring and documenting pays for the difference within a few builds.

print("Generic: unmarked strap, measure by eye, no system.")

title: Signature Desk Trunk System
description: The Signature desk method runs one trunk per desk edge — power one side, data the other — strapped every foot and anchored with the kit's adhesive mounts. title: Signature Test-Bench Cable Discipline
description: Open test benches are cable chaos by default. The Signature bench method anchors the PSU trunk to the bench edge with two anchors, straps each test lead's cable to its instrument, and color-codes by voltage rail — red 12V, yellow 5V, orange 3.3V. A bench that looks like a lab instead of a nest gets used more and miswired less.

t: Signature Strap Recycling and Refresh Cycle
title: Signature Strap Recycling and Refresh Cycle
description: Signature straps are rated for the refresh cycle: every major rebuild, peel all straps, pick the lint, test the peel, and retire the weak ones to non-critical duty (desk cables) while fresh straps take the case interior. The roll's predictable yield means you always know how many fresh straps a rebuild needs. Nothing weak holds anything important.

demo.program:
print("Rebuild refresh: peel all -> de-lint -> peel-test -> sort.")
print("Strong straps -> case interior. Weak straps -> desk duty or retired.")
print("Predictable roll yield: fresh-strap count per rebuild always known.")

title: Signature Tight-Bundle Technique
description: For the fattest PSU trunks, the Signature technique uses two straps in an X: one strap around the bundle, a second strap through the first's loop and around again, cinching in two axes. The X holds round trunks that a single strap lets go oval and loose. It is the kind of trick that only matters on 1000W-plus cable sets — exactly where it matters most.

demo.program:
print("X-strap: strap 1 around bundle, strap 2 through strap 1's loop, cinch.")
print("Holds round on fat PSU trunks where single straps go oval.")
print("Matters most on 1000W+ cable sets: exactly where it matters.")

title: Signature Label Strap: Write-On Hook-and-Loop
description: Signature label straps have a matte write-on patch fused to the strap's outer face — write the trunk's contents with a fine marker ('GPU PWR', 'SATA 1-3') and the label rides the bundle. Behind the tray, labels turn every trunk into a labeled system; under the desk, they end the 'which cable is this' tracing game. The patch wipes clean with alcohol for reuse.

print("Write-on patch fused to strap face: label the bundle ('GPU PWR').")

print("Alcohol wipe resets the patch: labels are reusable too.")

title: Signature Bundle Inspection Checklist
description: The Signature inspection runs before the side panel closes: every trunk strapped at 6-to-8-inch intervals, no strap tails flopping, service loops present and carded, colors correct per code, panel closes with zero pressure, and no cable touching fan blades. Six checks, two minutes, and the build's cable management is verified — not just hoped for.

demo.program:
checks = ["straps every 6-8 in", "no floppy tails", "service loops carded",
          "colors per code", "panel closes, zero pressure", "clear of fan blades"]
for i, c in enumerate(checks, 1):
    print(f"  [{i}] {c}")
print("Six checks, two minutes: verified, not hoped for.")
